questions_and_answers.question_text: What is the literal meaning of jiǔyǎng?
Why is jiǔyǎng not often used in the PRC?
Why is no le needed in the last sentence of exchange 5?
Write the Chinese for "How long have you been here?"
Write the Chinese for "It has been only two months since I came."
Where has the focus shifted to in the gāng sentence?

answers.answer_text: From the coming to the shortness of the period — the focus is on gāng.

questions_and_answers.question_text: What does jiǔyǎng imply about the two speakers?

answers.answer_text: A status difference — it is used when meeting someone of higher status.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Contrast Wǒ láile liǎngge yuè le with Wǒ gāng lái liǎngge yuè.

answers.answer_text: The first means "I have been here two months now"; the second stresses that it has been ONLY two months since I came.

articles.text:
5. B: Jiǔyǎng, jiǔyǎng.              Glad to meet you.
   B: Nín láile duō jiǔ le?          How long have you been here?
   C: Jiǔyǎng. Wǒ gāng lái           Glad to meet you. It has been only
      liǎngge yuè.                    two months since I came.

Notes on No. 5

Jiǔyǎng means, literally, "I have looked up to you for a long time" or "I have looked forward to meeting you." It is used when meeting someone of higher status. Because jiǔyǎng implies a status difference, the expression is not often used in the PRC.

Gāng, "only just": You have learned the sentence Wǒ láile liǎngge yuè le, "I have been here two months now." In the last sentence of exchange 5, notice that no le is needed. The focus has shifted from the coming to the shortness of the period; that is, the focus is on gāng.
